documentation.range: This species occurs in the Mekong basin in Viet Nam and Cambodia, south-eastern Thailand, the Malay Peninsula from Sungai Golok southwards, as well as in Borneo and Sumatra, Indonesia. This species was also introduced to Singapore (Blanc and D'Aubenton 1965, Kottelat et al. 1993, Kottelat and Lim 1995, Rainboth 1996). Individuals in Myanmar that were previously assigned to this species are now valid as S. inscriptus (Roberts 2012).
documentation.population:
The population of this species occurs at very low density throughout its range following significant declines in the past of well over 50% (M. Kottelat pers. comm. 2011). The overall population trend is thought to still be declining.

Local harvesters of juvenile Scleropages formosus interviewed in Cambodia in 2008 all reported that the abundance of this species had dramatically declined, with some populations thought to be locally extinct (Rowley et al. 2008). Based on these declines a population decline of up to 75% in Cambodia was estimated between 1997-2007. Catch statistics show declines of 90% in Cambodia, Thailand and the Malay Pensinsula since 2010 (C. Vidthayanon pers. comm. 2019).
documentation.habitats:
Scleropages formosus occurs in lakes, deep parts of swamps, flooded forests and stretches of deep rivers with slow currents and dense, overhanging vegetation (M. Kottelat pers. comm. 2011), as well as reservoirs and waterways (Yue et al. 2004). It is carnivorous and has a wide diet that includes insects, vertebrates, arachnids, small fish and even non-woody roots and tubers (Yue et al. 2004, Vidthayanon 2005).

It is a fairly large fish that can grow to 1 m in length and weigh over 7 kg (Yue et al. 2004). It has three colours morphs of red, green and gold which have distinct geographic distributions (Tang et al. 2004). It is also relatively long lived, reaching maturity at 2-4 years (Scott and Fuller 1976). It has a distinct breeding season (e.g. March-April in Cambodia (Rowley et al. 2008) and August in Malaysia (Scott and Fuller 1976)), where females produce 30-100 large eggs which are then protected in the mouth of males as fertilised eggs and larvae (Yue et al. 2004). There is a single ovary (Suleiman 2003). No longevity data exist for wild populations. However, its longevity is expected to be similar to Scleropages leichardti, which lives for 7-8 years (Pusey et al. 2004).
documentation.threats:
Scleropages formosus has been targeted for the international ornamental aquarium trade since the 1970s, and this intense collection pressure is thought to have caused population declines throughout its range. This species is particularly vulnerable to overharvesting due to its long life, late maturity and low fecundity (Yue et al. 2004). Harvesting methods can also be very destructive, as adult males are often killed using methods such as explosives or electro-fishing to make them release the juveniles, which are then collected and sold (Rowley et al. 2008). Trade in wild-caught individuals is now regulated, however enforcement is not optimal and there is still pressure on some wild populations, especially ones with colourful morphs such as red or gold. It is also caught incidentally in local fisheries. 

Another major threat to this species is from habitat degradation and loss caused by a variety of human activities. A number of its swamp habitats have been transformed into agricultural land for example, while large areas of forested habitat have been logged and transformed into plantations. In Indonesia, forest fires have heavily impacted peat swamp forests (M. Kottelat pers. comm. 2011). In Cambodia, freshwater habitats of this species are also under pressure from road development, mining and hydro-electrical dam development, with most of the river systems known to contain S. formosus under threat from dam construction (Rowley et al. 2008).
documentation.measures: This species has been listed on Appendix I of CITES since 1975. Commercial trading is only allowed for captive bred individuals (Mohd-Shamsudin et al. 2011), although an illegal trade in wild-caught individuals still exists. Cultured stocks exist in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and China (Yue et al. 2004). Parts of the range are within protected areas. There are some local community level conservation measures in place in countries such as Cambodia, where breeding areas have collection restrictions and are patrolled and monitored (Rowley et al. 2008).
documentation.use_trade:
Scleropages formosus is a very popular and valuable fish in the ornamental aquarium trade. Demand has increased substantially since the 1960s, with red or gold adults costing over $USD 20,000 in 2004 (Yue et al. 2004), and some rare forms even selling for over $USD 100,000 (Medipally et al. 2016).

This species is listed under Appendix I of CITES, which restricts the trade of wild caught individuals, although an illegal trade does still occur. Local harvesters in Cambodia could earn $USD 11-13 per juvenile in 2008, which were mainly exported to countries such as Thailand, although some went into the national aquarium trade. After the fry have been released, the adult males are sometimes also eaten as part of local subsistence fisheries (Rowley et al. 2008).

There are large cultured stocks of this species in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and China (Yue et al. 2004, Mu et al. 2011), which are exported to several nations. The production value of this species amounted to half of the total ornamental fish production in Malaysia in 2011/2012 (Medipally et al. 2016).
documentation.rationale:
The population of this species is at very low densities throughout its range following significant declines in the past. This has been a highly valued species in the international aquarium trade since the 1970s and has been listed on Appendix I of CITES since 1975. There are a number of registered CITES breeders in Asia and the specimens they produce can be imported into several nations. Other nations restrict or prohibit possession of this species. Illegal trade does occur. Habitat degradation throughout the species' range, caused by a variety of human activities, is now its main threat. For example, a number of swamp habitats have been transformed into agricultural land. Areas of forested habitat have been logged and transformed into plantations. Forest fires have impacted most of the species' range in Indonesia, especially peat swamp forests.

Populations in Cambodia, Thailand and the Malay Peninsula have declined by 90% since 2010 (C. Vidthayanon pers. comm. 2019) and populations in Cambodia were reported to be declining prior to this (Rowley et al. 2008) and are continuing to do so. Three generations are equivalent to 12-21 years and the decline is considered to be of at least the same magnitude over this period. No data on population trends are available for other parts of the range, but they are likely to be in decline given ongoing threats. If all other populations were stable then this would support a decline of approximately 45% and if all were declining at the same rate as those in Cambodia, Thailand and the Malay Peninsula this would support a decline of approximately 90%. Based on this, this species is assessed as Endangered as the majority of the range (50-80%) falls within the thresholds for this category. This population decline is based on a decline in area of occupancy, extent of occurrence and habitat quality, and levels of exploitation.

Given the ongoing habitat degradation in South-east Asia, more information is needed on the wild populations' status. Further taxonomic study is required to confirm the taxonomic status of populations of the species across its range.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Until 2003, all Scleropages from Southeast Asia were considered to belong to the same species; S. formosus. In 2003 Pouyaud et al., considered there to actually be four species, three of which they described as new (S. aureus, S. legendrei, S. macrocephalus). Kottelat and Widjanarti (2005) reviewed the published data and did not reach the same conclusions from the quality of the data presented, and in order for more than one species to be recognised, a professional standard study would need to be presented. In 2012, a new species (S. incriptus) was described from Myanmar (Roberts 2012).
